# Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling

Also called: Dynamic NeRF, Articulated NeRF, Human NeRF

## Overview
Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling extends static radiance fields to handle time-varying geometry and non-rigid deformations, primarily in human performance capture [G]. It solves the ill-posed problem of mapping dynamic 3D points to a static representation by introducing canonical spaces, skeletal constraints, or surface-relative encodings [G]. Unlike static methods, these approaches must jointly optimize or infer pose, deformation, and appearance from monocular or sparse multi-view video inputs [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map a 3D query point $\mathbf{x}$ observed at time $t$ to a canonical space $\mathbf{x}_c$ where the radiance field is static [G]. The rendering process remains volume rendering, but the density $\sigma$ and color $c$ are conditioned on the deformation state [G].

1.  **Canonical Transformation:** A transformation function $T(\mathbf{x}, t)$ maps observation space to canonical space [G]. Common strategies include:
    *   **Skeleton-based:** Using inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) or skeletal relative coordinates [[A-NeRF](18108-a-nerf.md)].
    *   **Surface-based:** Using signed distances to nearest neighbors in a reconstructed surface mesh [[SelfNeRF](18160-selfnerf.md)].
    *   **Residual-based:** Predicting radiance residuals in the canonical space conditioned on pose [[MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md)].
2.  **Conditioning:** The radiance field MLP $F_\omega$ takes the canonical point $\mathbf{x}_c$, view direction $\mathbf{v}$, and often a pose or identity code as input [G].
3.  **Optimization:** Training typically involves minimizing photometric loss $\| C_{rendered} - I_{gt} \|$ [G]. Articulated methods often include regularization terms for pose smoothness and consistency with initial pose estimates [[A-NeRF](18108-a-nerf.md)].

## Subtopics

### [MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md)
MoCo-NeRF models non-rigid body motions as radiance residual fields rather than spatial offsets, using rigid skeletal transformations as a prior. It separates the canonical radiance representation from pose-dependent non-rigid residuals, allowing direct supervision from ground-truth pixel colors. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial deformation fields, it avoids high computational complexity by operating directly in the radiance space. Choose it for monocular human video rendering where residual-based conditioning is preferred over spatial offsets.

### [Neural Scene Graphs](17706-neural-scene-graphs.md)
Neural Scene Graphs decomposes dynamic, multi-object scenes into a learned hierarchical scene graph with decoupled object transformations and scene representations. It lifts the assumption of static scene consistency required by existing neural rendering methods. Unlike methods that encode the entire scene into a single network, it uses object-level implicit representations learned from video frames and tracking data. Choose it for novel view synthesis of dynamic multi-object scenes with unseen arrangements.

### [A-NeRF](18108-a-nerf.md)
A-NeRF learns a user-specific neural 3D body model and underlying skeleton pose from unlabelled monocular videos by extending NeRFs with a skeleton for time-varying motion. It defines spatial latent variables relative to the pose of body parts to overcome ill-posed inverse operations. Unlike [MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md) which uses residual-based conditioning, it uses skeleton-relative embeddings; unlike [SelfNeRF](18160-selfnerf.md) which uses surface-based SDFs, it uses volumetric density conditioned on bone-relative coordinates. Choose it for unlabelled monocular human performance capture requiring joint pose and appearance optimization.

### [Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars (PVA)](18139-pixel-aligned-volumetric-avatars-pva.md)
PVA estimates a volumetric 3D avatar from a few input images of a human head, enabling view synthesis for unseen identities and expressions. It generalizes to new identities by combining neural radiance fields with local, pixel-aligned features extracted directly from input images, avoiding information loss associated with global latent codes. Unlike mesh-based methods, it captures arbitrary topology and high-frequency details without requiring explicit 3D supervision. Choose it for few-shot head avatar synthesis with arbitrary topology.

### [SelfNeRF](18160-selfnerf.md)
SelfNeRF is a novel view synthesis method for human performance that trains from scratch using monocular self-rotating video inputs, achieving high-fidelity results in approximately twenty minutes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md) and [A-NeRF](18108-a-nerf.md) by eliminating the need for multi-view inputs or explicit skeletal priors, instead relying on a surface-relative hash encoding to aggregate inter-frame information and accelerate training. Choose it for rapid training from monocular self-rotating videos without skeletal priors.

### [CLA-NeRF](20285-cla-nerf.md)
CLA-NeRF is a differentiable representation for articulated objects that explicitly models part and joint attributes, disentangling camera pose, part pose, part segmentation, and joint attributes to allow independent control during rendering. It solves the problem of rendering deformable articulated objects at unseen poses and estimating their articulated pose from RGB images, without requiring CAD models or depth data. Unlike standard NeRF formulations which model camera poses but ignore object articulation, it predicts a part segmentation field alongside density and color, enabling the inference of joint attributes via line-fitting on the segmentation field. Choose it for general articulated object rendering and pose estimation without known joint attributes.

### [Object-Centric Voxelization for Dynamic Scenes](20318-object-centric-voxelization-for-dynamic-scenes.md)
DynaVol is an unsupervised 3D dynamic scene decomposition method that unifies geometric structures and object-centric learning within a differentiable volume rendering framework. It solves the multi-view mismatch of 2D object segmentation by ensuring 3D consistency, enabling novel view synthesis, and allowing direct scene editing. Unlike 2D image decomposition methods such as SAVi, it infers a probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations via object-centric voxelization, facilitating fine-grained separation without geometric priors. Choose it for unsupervised 3D dynamic scene decomposition and direct editing.

### [MI-NeRF](21740-mi-nerf.md)
MI-NeRF is a method for learning a single unified dynamic neural radiance field (NeRF) that models complex non-rigid facial motion for multiple identities using only monocular videos of arbitrary length. It solves the problem of expensive per-identity optimization in dynamic face reconstruction by training a single implicit representation $F_\Theta$ conditioned on identity, expression, latent codes, position, and view direction. Unlike previous generic NeRF models that require static settings and multiple input views during training, it works for monocular videos captured in the wild, reducing total training time by up to 90% compared to standard single-identity NeRFs. Choose it for multi-identity dynamic face reconstruction from monocular videos.

### Neural Human Performer
A feed-forward method for synthesizing novel-view videos of arbitrary human performers from sparse multi-view camera inputs (3-4 views) by learning generalizable neural radiance fields using a parametric 3D body model (SMPL) and transformer-based aggregation of spatio-temporal features [S1, unofficial]. It constructs time-augmented skeletal features by leveraging SMPL and aggregates temporal information using a temporal transformer, followed by a multi-view transformer for cross-attention [S1, unofficial].

### HOSNeRF
A novel 360° free-view rendering method capable of reconstructing dynamic human-object-scene neural radiation fields from a single monocular video [S2]. It estimates complex object motion during human-object interaction by introducing new object skeletons into the traditional human skeletal hierarchy and uses two learnable object state embeddings for different interaction contexts [S2]. It significantly outperforms existing techniques on challenging datasets, with a 40% to 50% improvement on the LPIPS metric [S2].

### MonoNeRF
A method for learning generic dynamic radiation fields from monocular video [S2]. It learns both point features and scene streams through video feature extraction, implicit velocity fields, and stream-based feature aggregation modules [S2]. It supports new applications such as scene editing, unseen frame synthesis, and fast new scene adaptation [S2].

### Implicit Time-varying NeRF
Models deformations implicitly by conditioning the NeRF on a representation of the deformation state (e.g., a time input) [S3, unofficial]. Condition the volume on a vector that represents the deformed state [S3, unofficial]. Conditioning input is a time input (potentially positionally encoded) or an auto-decoded latent code per time step [S3, unofficial].

### NeRF with Deformation MLP
A method that uses a deformation MLP to model non-rigid scenes. It has no reliance on pre-computed scene information apart from camera parameters [S4, unofficial]. NR-NeRF generates slightly less sharp outputs compared to Nerfies [S4, unofficial].

### NeRF with Ray Bending for Non-Rigid Deformation
A method that achieves scene deformation by using ray bending, allowing for complex rendering effects like bullet-time (time slice/freeze effect) without explicit supervision for rigidity network learning [S5, unofficial]. Input consists of multiple images from a non-rigid scene with extrinsics and intrinsics [S5, unofficial]. A single canonical neural radiance volume is searched/found, which is deformed via ray bending to render colors [S5, unofficial]. Appearance and geometry information of the static canonical volume is weighted and parameterized with weights [S5, unofficial]. Deformation modeling collects information from straight rays sent from the camera and defines a deformation that presents the ray bending deformation processing [S5, unofficial]. Add MLP design on the ray bending with weight as input parameters [S5, unofficial]. Handle mapping processing on the static canonical volume, gaining form from a designed auto-decoded latent code [S5, unofficial]. Weakness: Takes a whole NeRF rendering network for a unit or independent object or scene rendering [S5, unofficial].

### Factored-NeRF
A method that computes static and dynamic fields independently to enable separate rendering, object trajectory mapping, and non-rigid movement adaptation [S6]. Leverage annotations from keyframes and propagate them to adjacent frames to deduce scene flows, map object trajectories, and determine rigidities [S6]. Perform comprehensive end-to-end optimization to modify object placements, trajectories, and adapt to non-rigid movements [S6].

### Video-NeRF
Leverage monocular video depth estimation to constrain time-varying geometry within a globally consistent representation [S7, unofficial]. Model scene dynamics by encoding time information into the MLP, concatenating temporal data with spatial coordinates and view direction [S7, unofficial]. Aggregate frame-wise 2.5D representations and propagate scene contents across time using a static scene loss [S7, unofficial].

## Background
The extension of NeRF to dynamic scenes originated with the need to capture human performance and articulated objects from limited camera views [G]. Early works like [A-NeRF](18108-a-nerf.md) addressed the ill-posed nature of monocular dynamic reconstruction by introducing skeletal-relative encodings and joint optimization of pose and appearance [S2]. Subsequent methods like [MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md) and [SelfNeRF](18160-selfnerf.md) refined this by decoupling rigid and non-rigid components or leveraging surface geometry for faster convergence. Generalizable approaches like Neural Human Performer [S1, unofficial] and HOSNeRF [S2] further expanded the domain to sparse multi-view and single-view human-object interactions, respectively.
